claims.claim: Portuguese raiders attacked captives at Arguin Bank in 1444 while shouting Christian battle cries, killing and capturing all they could.
claims.verbatim: But they, shouting out 'St. James', 'St. George', 'Portugal', at once attacked them, killing and taking all they could.
claims.source: Beazley & Prestage Hakluyt Vol I, Ch XIX, p. 65-66
claims.anchor: ### Verbatim quote A — The Christian battle cry attack (✅ VERIFIED)

claims.claim: During the 1444 Arguin raid, families were separated as parents fled and hid or buried children among seaweed trying to escape capture.
claims.verbatim: Then might you see mothers forsaking their children, and husbands their wives, each striving to escape as best he could. Some drowned themselves in the water; others thought to escape by hiding under their huts; others stowed their children among the sea-weed, where our men found them afterwards, hoping they would thus escape notice.
claims.source: Beazley & Prestage Hakluyt Vol I, Ch XIX, p. 66
claims.anchor: ### Verbatim quote B — The family separation (✅ VERIFIED)

claims.claim: The 1444 Arguin raid captured 165 men, women, and children, in addition to those killed.
claims.verbatim: They took captive of those Moors, what with men, women, and children, **165**, besides those that perished and were killed.
claims.source: Beazley & Prestage Hakluyt Vol I, Ch XIX, p. 66
claims.anchor: ### Outcome of the 1444 raid

claims.claim: At the Lagos auction two weeks after the Arguin raid, Prince Henry personally divided his royal fifth of the captives among his retinue.
claims.verbatim: The Infant was there, mounted upon a powerful steed, and accompanied by his retinue, making distribution of his favours, as a man who sought to gain but small treasure from his share; for of the forty-six souls that fell to him as his fifth, he made a very speedy partition of these...
claims.source: Beazley & Prestage Hakluyt Vol I, Ch XXV, p. 83

claims.claim: In a July 1526 letter, King Afonso I of Kongo protested that Portuguese merchants were seizing his countrymen, nobles, and vassals daily, depopulating his land.
claims.verbatim: And this harm has come to us at such cost that the said merchants take our countrymen the sons of our land and the sons of our noblemen every day, as well as our vassals and parents, because the thieves and men of bad conscience captivate them with a desire to have the things and goods of this Kingdom of which they are greedy, they seize and sell them in such a way, Sir, that because of this corruption and licentiousness, our land is being all but depopulated.
claims.source: French, Born in Blackness, p. 296
claims.anchor: ### Verbatim quote A — The depopulation protest (✅ VERIFIED)

claims.claim: King Afonso I of Kongo demanded in writing that all slave trading and export from his kingdom cease entirely.
claims.verbatim: Our will is that in this Kingdom there be no slave trade nor [any] outlet for it.
claims.source: French, Born in Blackness, p. 296
claims.anchor: ### Verbatim quote B — The trade-ban demand (✅ VERIFIED)

claims.claim: Afonso I's October 1526 letter described free Kongolese nobles and relatives being stolen and, once in traders' power, branded with fire and shackled in irons.
claims.verbatim: Many of our people... steal many of our free and protected people... they have stolen nobles and the sons of nobles, and our own relatives... and as soon as they are in the power of these white men they are at once branded with fire and clapped in irons.
claims.source: French, p. 296, citing Levy Maria Jordão, Historia do Congo (Lisbon: Typ. da Academia, 1877), pp. 56-58
claims.anchor: ### Synth-beat material (October 18, 1526 second letter — ✅ VERIFIED)

claims.claim: King João III of Portugal replied to Afonso's protest by dismissing the depopulation claim, implying Kongo's population size proved no captives had actually left.
claims.verbatim: You say in your letters that you do not want there to be any slave trade in your kingdom because it is depopulating your land. I can believe that you only say this as a result of the suffering that the Portuguese cause you, because I am told of the great size of Kongo and how it is so populated that it appears that not a single slave has left it.
claims.source: Malyn Newitt, The Portuguese in West Africa, 1415–1670: A Documentary History (Cambridge UP, 2010), Doc 36

claims.claim: Enslavement produced a two-tiered price structure: a newly captured person was priced cheaply based on the cost of capturing them, while a 'seasoned' slave commanded a much higher price.
claims.verbatim: The process of enslavement resulted in a two-tiered price structure, distinguishing the very low price of a newly taken captive (a price based not on the value of the person but on the cost of capturing him or her), and the higher price of a slave ready to be put to work.
claims.source: Patrick Manning, Slavery and African Life, Cambridge UP, 1990, ch. 4

claims.claim: Pope Nicholas V's 1455 bull Romanus Pontifex authorized reducing conquered non-Christian peoples to perpetual slavery.
claims.verbatim: ...illorumque personas in perpetuam servitutem redigendi...
claims.source: Davenport, European Treaties bearing on the History of the United States and its Dependencies to 1648, Vol. I (Carnegie Institution, 1917), p. 16

claims.claim: Romanus Pontifex authorized Portugal to invade, capture, and subdue Saracens, pagans, and enemies of Christ, seize their goods and lands, and reduce their persons to perpetual slavery.
claims.verbatim: ...to invade, search out, capture, vanquish, and subdue all Saracens and pagans whatsoever, and other enemies of Christ wheresoever placed, and the kingdoms, dukedoms, principalities, dominions, possessions, and all movable and immovable goods whatsoever held and possessed by them and **to reduce their persons to perpetual slavery**, and to apply and appropriate to himself and his successors the kingdoms, dukedoms, counties, principalities, dominions, possessions, and goods, and to convert them to his and their use and profit...

claims.claim: The English word 'slave' derives from 'Slav,' reflecting the Genoese and Venetian trade in captive Slavic peoples from the Black Sea region centuries before the Atlantic system.
claims.verbatim: Italians had established slave-trading ports along the northern coast of the Black Sea, much as later European merchants would do along the western coast of Africa. Over the course of nearly two and a half centuries the Genoese and the Venetians purchased thousands of captive Armenians, Circassians, Mingrelians, Tatars, and Bulgarians—**peoples whose vague ethnic status as 'Slavs' became the origin of the words for slave in western European languages**. 'Slav' slaves were highly prized from Muslim Egypt and Syria to Sicily and eastern Spain... In Sicily a notary's record in Latin referred to **sclavi negri, literally 'black Slavs,'** who outnumbered white slaves there by the 1490s.
claims.source: David Brion Davis, foreword to Eltis & Richardson, Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (Yale UP, 2010), p. xiv

claims.claim: Olaudah Equiano's account of Igbo society describes a strict rule requiring proof that anyone sold into slavery was a prisoner of war or convicted criminal, not simply captured at will.
claims.verbatim: They always carry slaves through our land; but the strictest account is exacted of their manner of procuring them before they are suffered to pass. Sometimes indeed we sold slaves to them, but they were only prisoners of war, or such among us as had been convicted of kidnapping, for adultery, and some other crimes, which we esteemed heinous.
claims.source: Equiano, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, 3rd ed. (London, 1790), pp. 13-14
